beats.say: Week twelve: measuring what matters. Nicky Barton, Head of Marketing Science at Mutinex, on how marketers work out what actually works.
Mutinex helps brands find what drives sales. GrowthOS reads the market, Nicky's team translates, and brands decide where the next dollar goes.
London, 1854. Cholera spread through Soho and experts blamed bad air. But data on where the deaths happened pointed to the water.
Marketing had the same problem. For decades it ran on surveys, sales data months late, and the gut feel of the most senior person in the room.
Then tracking grew. Banner ads showed clicks, AdWords intent, analytics visits, Facebook and the iPhone who you are, and the pixel what you buy.
So last touch became the default: the last click gets all the credit. It's a group assignment where whoever hits submit gets the whole mark.
Picture this shopper. She saw a billboard, heard the radio, then clicked a search ad. The billboard gets zero credit, the search ad a hundred percent.
So budgets flow to the bottom of the funnel, brand looks useless, and mental availability shrinks. Nike went direct, pulled back from retail, and people stopped seeing it.
Then privacy broke tracking. Safari limits, GDPR, then Apple's ask app not to track pop-up. Meta estimated that one pop-up cost it ten billion dollars in a year.

beats.say: Ask every platform how much it sold and the answers add up to over a hundred percent. Everyone did the assignment.
Enter marketing mix modelling. Weekly sales, media spend, price, promotions, seasons, the economy and competitors go in. Out come what drove sales, ROI by channel and the next dollar.
It's probabilistic, not deterministic. Not this click caused this sale, but the most likely effect, and how sure we are. More honest, and privacy safe.
A cafe on a busy corner gets walk-ins with zero ads. That's baseline. And ads keep working after they stop, like a song stuck in your head.
Add the fifth slice of pizza: returns diminish. Last year's star channel may not be the next best bet. And test first, like a flight simulator.

Across eighty-three brands in Australia and New Zealand, many drifted to performance. Those keeping brand muscle grew most. Yet cinema, radio and free-to-air, the longest lasting channels, were cut first.
If you can't add budget, don't add channels. Spreading money thinner shrinks results, and brands that go off air pay later.
Measurement has moved from the marketing report to the boardroom. The CEO asks what revenue and profit this created, and the CFO trusts the budget.
The numbers get easier to produce, so judgement becomes the job. The best marketers bring curiosity, comfort with numbers, commercial sense and storytelling.
So: last touch misleads, privacy broke tracking, and modelling reads the whole market. Keep your brand muscle, and always ask, how do we know it worked? That's week twelve.
